title: context-shunt v1 external artifact import contract
description: The normalized form of an external producer's manifest. A producer that already persists an oversized tool result to a file can hand that result to context-shunt without the host having to intercept the result itself. Every field here is untrusted input: it is validated against this schema, then re-proven against the filesystem and the artifact's own bytes before any handle exists. The contract is deliberately producer-agnostic - `producer.manifest_schema` names the foreign schema a profile translated from, so no particular producer's identifiers appear in the core API. There is no free-text field anywhere in this document: every string is a bounded token, so nothing from an untrusted manifest can ride into an envelope, a log line or a metric label.

import_contract.description: The revision of this contract the document declares. A document declaring an unknown revision is refused rather than read on a best-effort basis.

created_at.description: When the producer wrote the artifact. Advisory only: TTL is owned by the store and is measured from import, never from this value.

producer.description: Who produced the artifact, as bounded opaque tokens. `id` distinguishes one producer deployment from another in the import allowlist; `manifest_schema` is the foreign schema identifier a profile normalized from, kept so an import receipt can say what shape it came from without the core owning that shape.

artifact.description: Where the raw payload is and what it is claimed to be. `path` must canonicalize inside a configured import root, be a regular non-symlinked file, and survive the same source policy an ordinary capture does. `bytes` and `sha256` are claims: both are re-derived from the bytes actually read and a disagreement refuses the import rather than trusting either side.

origin.description: What produced the payload upstream. `tool` is a bounded token used only for operator-facing attribution; `upstream_truncated` decides which accounting baseline applies, because a payload the producer already shortened can only be credited at its observed size.
